h1:
Things to Do in Ayutthaya
Temples, Palaces, Markets and a Sunset Boat Loop
intro: Ayutthaya sits just over an hour from Bangkok, but the moment you walk into the historical park it feels like stepping into another era. The old island city is ringed by three rivers, and packs in ancient World Heritage temples, a royal summer palace, floating markets to graze through, and longtail boats that loop the island at dusk. We've rounded up the places actually worth your time, a mix of every style, with entry fees and opening hours updated so you can plan a trip straight off this list.

blocks.html: What makes Ayutthaya fun is how compact it is. Most of the major temples sit on the same island, so you can cycle or hop in a tuk-tuk and tick them off in a single day. Bang Pa-In Palace and the floating markets are just off the island, a short drive away, and if you have two days it's a lot more relaxed. We've split things into four groups to keep it clear: temples in the park, palaces, floating markets, and the boat loop around the island.

blocks.text: World Heritage temples in the historical park

blocks.html: Ayutthaya Historical Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The park itself is free to walk through, but each main temple charges around ฿50 to enter. If you plan to do several, the combined 6-temple ticket at ฿220 works out cheaper. Most are open 8:00–17:00.

items.name: Wat Mahathat — the Buddha head in the tree roots
items.blurb: This is the iconic Ayutthaya shot — a sandstone Buddha head wrapped in the roots of a banyan tree until the two have become one. Everyone stops to photograph it. By custom you should crouch down so your head sits lower than the Buddha's when you take the picture. The rest of the grounds have plenty more old prangs and ruined chedis to wander.

items.name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram — riverside Khmer style
items.blurb: One of the most beautiful temples in Ayutthaya. The Khmer-style central prang is ringed by smaller satellite prangs, set right on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River. In the late afternoon the golden light hits it beautifully, and it's a hugely popular spot for people in traditional Thai dress coming to shoot photos.
items.meta: Open 8:00–18:00 · off the island, west side

items.name: Wat Phra Si Sanphet — the three chedis
items.blurb: Once the temple inside the old royal palace grounds, with no resident monks. The highlight is the row of three Sri Lankan–style chedis that have become a symbol of the city. It sits in the centre of the island, an easy walk on from the Phra Mongkhon Bophit hall.

items.name: Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon — the big robed chedi
items.blurb: You can climb to the top of the large main chedi and look down on the reclining Buddha and the rows of Buddha images draped in yellow robes around the base. People come here to pray and ask for blessings, so it has a livelier feel than the ruined temples. It's off the island on the east side.
items.meta: Open 8:00–17:00 · off the island, east side

items.name: Wat Lokayasutharam — the open-air reclining Buddha
items.blurb: A large stucco reclining Buddha lying out in the open, over 40 metres long. People usually come to drape it in robes and pose for photos. It's free to enter and sits on the island not far from Wat Phra Si Sanphet, so it's an easy stop to add.

items.name: Wat Ratchaburana — climb down into the crypt
items.blurb: Right next to Wat Mahathat. The draw here is climbing up the prang and then down a narrow staircase into the crypt chamber, where Ayutthaya-era gold treasures were once found. Anyone claustrophobic might struggle with the tight space, but if you like a bit of exploring you'll love it.

blocks.title: A tip on entry fees
blocks.html: If you plan to do 5 temples or more, the combined 6-temple ticket at ฿220 beats paying ฿50 at each one. You can buy it at any of the main temples and just show it when you enter the next one.

items.label: Day trips from Ayutthaya
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.html: Ayutthaya was once the royal capital, so it has palaces both inside and outside the old city. These two feel completely different: one is a beautiful summer palace that's still in use, the other an old palace that's now a museum.

items.name: Bang Pa-In Royal Palace
items.blurb: A summer palace on the bank of the Chao Phraya, with sprawling gardens and a mix of Thai, European and Chinese architecture, including a photogenic pavilion sitting out on the water. Open 8:00–16:00, ฿30 for Thais and ฿100 for foreigners. It's off the island to the south, and dress is modest — cover shoulders and knees. There are wraps to borrow at the entrance.

items.name: Chankasem Palace (the Front Palace)
items.blurb: An old palace in the centre of town that's now a national museum, displaying antiquities and stories from the Ayutthaya period. It's a good fit if you want some historical context before walking the temples. It's on the island in the northeast corner, and closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

blocks.html: Ayutthaya has several floating markets. They're tourist markets built to give an old-world feel rather than traditional working markets, but they're fun to graze through and photograph, and make a good afternoon stop before an evening boat trip.

items.name: Ayothaya Floating Market
items.blurb: The biggest floating market in Ayutthaya, spread over roughly 13 hectares with hundreds of shops and boats selling goods. You can graze on savoury and sweet Thai snacks, watch period performances, and catch historical shows. Open daily 9:00–18:00, off the island on the east side near Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon.

items.name: Khlong Sa Bua Floating Market
items.blurb: Smaller and more easygoing, leaning into local snacks and Thai sweets. It's less crowded than Ayothaya, which suits anyone who wants to stroll at a relaxed pace without jostling with big tourist crowds.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: The floating markets in Ayutthaya are set up for tourism, not traditional village life. If you come expecting cheap local-market food you might be disappointed, but if you're here for the old-world atmosphere and photos, they're a good time.

blocks.text: A sunset loop around the island by boat

blocks.html: The Ayutthaya island city is ringed by three rivers — the Chao Phraya, the Pa Sak and the Lopburi. Taking a longtail boat around the island in the early evening is a great way to see the city once the sun is lower, catching several riverside temples from angles you can't reach on foot, especially Wat Chaiwatthanaram at sunset.

items: Private charter, 1 hour — around ฿1,000–1,500 per boat if you haggle at the pier, seating 6–8 people. Some operators charge ฿2,500–3,000 for a boat with a guide.
Public boat, 2 hours — around ฿200 per person, cheaper and good if you're travelling solo or as a couple.
Popular route — loops past Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Wat Phutthaisawan and Wat Phanan Choeng, home to a giant seated Buddha.
Best timing — set off about an hour before sunset to get both the evening light and the temples reflected in the water.

blocks.title: Agree the price before you board
blocks.html: Charter prices at the pier are negotiable. Settle the price and the route before you get on, and spell out which temples you'll pass and how many stops, so there are no surprises at the end of the trip.

blocks.text: Planning an Ayutthaya trip that fits

items: Just one day — do the on-island temples (Mahathat, Ratchaburana, Phra Si Sanphet, Phra Mongkhon Bophit) from morning into the afternoon, then finish with an evening boat loop.
Two days — day one for the on-island temples plus a floating market, day two heading off the island to Bang Pa-In, Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon, and Wat Chaiwatthanaram in the evening.
Getting there — from Bangkok it's about an hour by train or minivan. In town, rent a bicycle, hire a tuk-tuk by the hour, or rent a motorbike.
What to wear — temples and palaces require covered shoulders and knees. Bring a hat and water, since the park gets strong sun with little shade.

faq.q: Can you do Ayutthaya in one day?
faq.a: Yes, if you focus on the on-island temples — Wat Mahathat, Wat Ratchaburana, Wat Phra Si Sanphet and the Phra Mongkhon Bophit hall, which are all close together. You can cycle or take a tuk-tuk and tick them off in a day, then finish with an evening boat trip. Save Bang Pa-In and the floating markets for a second day.

faq.q: How much is temple entry in Ayutthaya?
faq.a: Most main temples charge around ฿50 each, while the park itself is free to walk through. If you plan to do several, the combined 6-temple ticket at ฿220 is better value. Some temples, like Wat Lokayasutharam, are free.

faq.q: Which temple is the most beautiful in Ayutthaya?
faq.a: Many people give it to the riverside Wat Chaiwatthanaram — a Khmer-style prang ringed by satellite prangs, gorgeous in the evening light. Wat Mahathat stands out for the Buddha head in the tree roots, the iconic image of the city.

faq.q: Are the Ayutthaya floating markets worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes if you like an old-world atmosphere and grazing on snacks, but understand they're built for tourism rather than traditional village life. Ayothaya Floating Market is the biggest, open 9:00–18:00, and makes a good afternoon stop.

faq.q: How much does a boat trip around the island cost?
faq.a: A private 1-hour charter runs around ฿1,000–1,500 per boat if you haggle at the pier, seating 6–8 people. A 2-hour public boat is around ฿200 per person. We'd set off about an hour before sunset to catch the evening light.
